entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: One definition of filed, because two of the three were wrong
entries.body:
The Today page said a message needed filing and the Inbox it linked to said
nothing did. Both were reading the same row: Dan's note to Brian Silver, filed
to TransUnion the day before. The Inbox knew that counted; Today and Pipeline
were still matching on applicationId alone, so a message filed to an employer
stayed in their counts permanently. The only way to clear the badge was to file
the message somewhere it did not belong.

Filing to a company exists precisely because Brian's introduction belongs to
TransUnion whether or not TransUnion ever posts a role. A count that disagrees
with the page behind it teaches him to stop trusting counts, which is the one
thing the Today page cannot afford.

The query was written out three times and fixed in one of them. It is a single
exported predicate now, so the next fix reaches every caller. Verified against
the database first (the Inbox already said zero) and then in the browser: the
headline went from two things to one and the Inbox card reads clean.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: The signature is in the editor, so the checkbox stops being a promise
entries.body:
Dan's thank-you to Ted went out unsigned with the box ticked. The cause was a
rule that reads sensibly and is wrong for one case: editing a draft switched
the signature off, on the reasoning that a draft already contains one. A
FORWARDED draft does not. It carries a signature inside the quote and none of
its own, so the note went out with his sign-off nowhere in the part he wrote.

The deeper fault is that the signature was appended at save and never shown.
The checkbox was a claim about what would happen later, so when it was wrong
there was nothing on screen to contradict it. It is real text in the editor
now, present from the first paint the way a mail client shows it, and what
goes out is what he can see.

The original design existed to stop two failure modes, and both are now the
toggle's job rather than avoided by not trying. A marked block plus
strip-from-the-marker-to-the-end covers them, verified on six cases: on, on
twice, off, switching the address label, off again, and a forward whose quoted
original contains an unmarked signature of its own. Turning it off restores
the body byte for byte, including the quote.

Editing a draft now asks whether it is signed instead of assuming, which the
marker makes answerable. On by default, remembered in localStorage, and the
composer resets to a signed empty message after a save rather than an empty
one with the box ticked and nothing under it.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Forward to anyone, including someone who is not a contact yet
entries.body:
Two things Dan asked for, and the second is what makes the first useful.

Forwarding now offers "Someone new...", which takes a name, an email and a
company. With an introduction that is the normal case rather than the
exception: the person being thanked is often newer to the search than the
person who was written to, and requiring them to exist first means leaving the
thread, making a contact, coming back and finding the message again.

The employer is recorded on the contact AND created as a Company row when it
is new, so the person appears under an employer that exists rather than under
a name nothing else knows about. Matched case-insensitively, like mail filing,
so a typed "transunion" joins the real TransUnion instead of forking it -
verified: creating a contact at TransUnion left the company count unchanged.
An address already on file resolves to that contact rather than a second copy,
since duplicates are how a thread ends up split in two.

And forwarding lands IN the draft. It used to leave one on somebody else's
page and Dan on the page he started from, with the actual point of a forward
still to do on a screen he had to go and find: the note written on top is the
only part addressed to the new recipient. The action redirects to
?edit=<draftId>, the page loads that draft, and the composer holds it on first
paint - seeded from the prop rather than in an effect, so the empty box never
renders first.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Companies are reachable, and filing to one that has no posting works
entries.body:
Dan filed a message to a company and nothing appeared to happen. It had
worked: the row stayed in the inbox because "filed" was defined as
applicationId being set, so a company-filed message still matched the to-file
query. A write that leaves the screen unchanged is the same as a broken
button. Filed now means filed against either, the Filed list carries both, and
a company-filed row links to the company rather than to an application it does
not have.

He also asked the question the feature could not survive: what if the company
has no posting? The picker listed only employers with a live application,
which excludes by definition the case this exists for - an introduction to
somebody at a company he has never applied to. It lists every company now, and
"A company not listed..." creates one, matched case-insensitively first so
"transunion" does not become a second TransUnion.

And there was no way to reach a company at all except by opening one of its
postings and clicking the name, which makes an employer with no posting
unreachable. /companies now exists and is in the nav: 85 employers, the ones
with no roles tracked included, with their people and message counts.

Filing is one control with a toggle rather than two forms side by side. They
are one decision with two answers - filing to a company clears the role - and
two forms implied you might do both.

Mail filed to a company links to a person. The sender match alone was not
enough: half of what lands here is Dan's own sent mail synced back, so the
sender is him and there is nobody to open. It falls back to the sole contact
at that employer, and only when there is exactly one, since guessing between
two people is worse than not linking.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Forward a sent note, and file mail against a company with no role behind it
entries.body:
Two gaps Dan hit within an hour of using the app for real.

FORWARDING. Ted introduced him to Brian, Dan wrote to Brian, and Ted deserves
thanking. Copying Ted would have been the lazy version and a worse one: it
turns a one-to-one note into a three-way conversation, Brian answers more
carefully knowing the introducer is reading, and a cc is not a thank-you, it
is evidence. Forward opens a draft on the other person with the original
quoted and its attachments carried, because "here is what I sent him" without
the resume is not what was sent. It creates a draft rather than sending, since
the note on top is the entire point. A draft cannot be forwarded: that would
show someone a message its supposed recipient has never seen.

COMPANY FILING. A networking introduction has no application behind it. Brian
is a person at TransUnion, not a job, so filing that mail under a role would
invent one and leaving it unfiled loses it. MailMessage takes a companyId, the
inbox offers "File to company" beside the role picker, and the company page
grows a section for mail that belongs to the employer rather than to one of
its roles - without somewhere to show it, filing would be the same as losing.

Filing to a role now records the company too, through one helper rather than
at each of the three call sites that set applicationId. Any one of them that
forgot would leave a message the company page cannot see.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Cc, Bcc, and a copy to yourself before it goes to a stranger
entries.body:
Dan is drafting a note to a TransUnion executive and wanted to copy people and
check the message first. Both are on the draft row, where the send decision is
actually made, so an existing draft gets them without being rewritten.

Cc and Bcc are typed or picked from a datalist of every contact plus his own
addresses. Deliberately free text rather than contact ids: a cc is often an
assistant who is not a contact and never will be, and forcing a Contact row to
copy someone is friction on the one path where friction costs a relationship.
They are stored on the draft, so what he decided while writing survives until
he sends, which can be days.

Every address is validated at send time and one bad entry stops the whole
send. Gmail will accept a header containing a malformed address and simply not
deliver to it, which is the worst available outcome: the message goes, the app
reports success, and neither Dan nor the person he meant to copy ever knows.

"Send me a copy" sends the assembled message - same subject, body, formatting
and attachments, same code path - to one of his own addresses. Two properties
make it safe. The destination is checked against his profile and the connected
mailbox rather than taken from the request, so it cannot misfire into the real
recipient; verified by trying to test-send to Brian and being refused. And it
returns before the draft is marked sent, so a test leaves a draft a draft -
this route is the only thing allowed to claim something was sent, and a test
was not.

The Bcc header is asserted on the assembled message rather than trusted:
getting it wrong exposes an address that was meant to be hidden.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Stop the app writing its own letterhead, and refuse to send without a subject
entries.body:
Dan sent the first email out of this app and both faults were mine.

THE SUBJECT. The send route fell back to "Note to ${recipientName}" when the
subject box was empty, and that is what a TransUnion executive received as the
subject line of a networking introduction. "Company - Role" is a defensible
default for an application; an internal-sounding label for a person is not.
The route refuses to send with no subject now. It is the only code path
allowed to claim something was sent, so it is the right place to refuse to
send something wrong.

THE PLACEHOLDERS. The master resume carried "Southport, CT · [phone] ·
[email] · [LinkedIn]" as its contact line, because buildMasterResume asked the
model to write the header. No other document here does that: every tailored
resume gets its letterhead from buildContactBlock, from his actual profile.
Asked for a contact line, a model writes brackets. The master and the
introduction letter both take the real header now, the model starts at
EXECUTIVE PROFILE, and anything it writes above that is stripped. The letter
had a hardcoded address string, which is the same fault wearing different
clothes - a second copy of his details that goes stale in silence.

fileGeneralDocument refuses to file a document containing a bracket
placeholder at all. These are the two documents with no posting behind them
and no review step in front, sent by hand to people, so the check belongs in
code and not in a prompt.

Also the name sat 2pt above the contact line, which at 17pt reads as touching.
140 twips in docx, 7pt in the PDF.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Open the master letter on who he is, and attach both to a contact in one click
entries.body:
Two things from Dan, plus the "---" that started it.

The horizontal rules were the model writing markdown out of habit into a
format that has no rule for them, so they fell through to "paragraph" and
rendered as three literal hyphens with paragraph spacing. Dropped in the
parser rather than at one call site, so an imported or adopted document gets
the same treatment, and the builder is told not to write them. Worth being
straight about the rest of it though: removing five lines did not take the
master off page three. It is 1,595 words and 31 bullets, and the rendered PDF
is three pages - counted from the PDF's own page objects rather than estimated
from word count, which has been wrong here in both directions. Three pages is
what "deep, highlight all of my experience" produces, and it is right for a
master.

The letter now opens where Dan said it should: a seasoned executive with deep
Fortune 100 experience, naming Delta and Charter, and the agency years at
dentsu McGarryBowen, VML and Ogilvy. Those were being left out entirely, and
they are the reason he can sit with a CMO and a CTO in the same meeting.

And both documents attach to any contact in one click. This needed no change
to the send route at all: it already resolves attachments by Drive file id,
and that is exactly what a general document is. The composer offers the PDF,
since that is what a stranger opens without thinking and the Word copy is for
editing rather than sending.

Brian Silver at TransUnion added as a contact with the introduction from Ted
recorded, since that call is today.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Put the send-anywhere documents in the UI, with the folder they live in
entries.body:
Dan asked where they were and could he get at them from the app. Fair: I told
him they were "at the top of your Jobs folder" and handed over nothing, which
is the same fault as a count that links nowhere.

Worse, he could not find the folder at all, and the reason is structural
rather than a mistake. The Drive connection is an address.com and the mailbox
is an addressgmail.com - two accounts on purpose, because the archive already
lived in the Workspace one. Opened from the other Google login the Jobs folder
simply is not there. Both Profile and Settings now link straight to it and say
which account it belongs to, so the next person to wonder is not left guessing.

The documents themselves are a small model of their own rather than
Documents-with-a-null-application: every list read here filters through the
application relation, so making that nullable would mean auditing all of them
to keep a general resume out of a role's history. GeneralDocument holds the
content and the two Drive ids, upserted per kind, and rebuilding updates the
same files so a link already sent keeps working - verified by rebuilding the
letter and getting the same two ids back.

Profile now shows both with word counts, Word and PDF links and a Rebuild, and
the rebuild refuses anything under 600 characters. A short generation
overwriting the one resume he hands out by hand is exactly the cover-letter
loss again, on the document with the least margin for it.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: A master resume and an introduction letter, and the house language rules enforced
entries.body:
Dan has a networking call today and needed something to send when there is no
role to tailor to. Two documents now sit at the top of the Jobs folder rather
than inside a company folder, because they belong to no application:

Dan_Curis_Resume_Master - merged from all four lane variants rather than cut
from one. A tailored resume selects sixteen bullets for a posting; the master
is the opposite document, so it keeps every distinct fact and lands at 1,600
words, 31 bullets, about three pages. That is correct for what it is: the full
record, and the thing every tailored version is cut from. Also written back to
Profile.masterResume.

Dan_Curis_Introduction_General - the "this is me" letter, three paragraphs,
no employer named and deliberately no greeting, since he adds one for the
person he has just spoken to. The first attempt opened "Dear Hiring Team" and
signed off twice, which is what happens when a letter builder written for
applications is pointed at something that is not one.

uploadGeneralDocument files both at the archive root and updates in place, so
the links stay stable.

And the language rules are enforced instead of requested. "No em-dashes" and
"US spelling" have been in the prompts from the start; toUSSpelling ran in
exactly one route and nothing removed a literal em-dash anywhere.
enforceHouseLanguage now runs on generation and on refine, the three rules are
stated in standingPreferences, and audit.ts checks documents for both. It
immediately found four cover letters carrying 31 em-dashes between them, all
adopted from Drive and written before Counsel existed; normalised, no words
changed.

Not enforced mechanically: sentences ending in a preposition. That needs
judgement about the whole clause and a mechanical fix would produce worse
sentences than it repaired, so it is a prompt rule and a review finding.

The audit check needed tightening twice before it earned its place - a
"-ising" suffix rule flagged "raising", and an "analys" stem flagged "analyst".
An audit that cries wolf gets ignored.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Act on Gemini's UI critique: four of five were right
entries.body:
Dan ran the app past Gemini. Taking each in turn, because one was wrong and
saying so matters as much as fixing the rest.

WRONG: that "the date doesn't auto-update" contradicts the app moving a status
from mail. Those are different fields. Nothing writes lastCheckedAt - checked
across the whole source - so the copy is accurate. Gemini conflated the date
with the status, which the app does update automatically and says so in the
activity log.

RIGHT, and the worst of them: "Apply" rendered on roles already at
INTERVIEWING. FindPostingButton never received the status; it showed Apply
whenever a posting link existed. It now takes the status, offers Apply only
before an application exists and "Open the posting" after, and the
download-two-documents side effect fires only in the apply case - rereading a
posting before an interview should not dump files into Downloads. Four labels
across two components collapsed to two clear ones: the posting button owns
"the posting", LinkedIn search says LinkedIn.

RIGHT: three model pickers on one page, the same five names rendered three
times. Fixed in the shared component so all nine call sites change together
and the next one cannot reintroduce it. But Dan pushed back on the first
version, and he was right: he uses this to send one resume to Gemini, so a
collapsed control labelled "model" would be a loss. It names the model that
will actually run - "Sonnet 5" until overridden, the override after - and
expands on click. Page went from three exposed pickers to zero.

RIGHT, and it was my own inconsistency from this morning: Drive authentication
sat on Profile while the folder it writes to sat on Settings. Moving only
Drive would have left the same split, so the mailbox went too - connecting an
account is wiring, and Profile is what the app knows about Dan. Both sections
now live under Accounts in Settings and the OAuth callback returns there.
Profile lost three connection queries it no longer feeds.

Fifth, on document buttons, is a real point I have not fixed yet: the repeated
.docx/.pdf/Restore controls carry no accessible name distinguishing one
version from another.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: The never-consider list is Dan's, and it was quietly enforcing his non-compete
entries.body:
He asked long ago that his non-compete not factor into evaluating roles. It
was, permanently and invisibly. "Southwest Airlines (non-compete competitor)"
sat on the ruled-out list, and that list is handed to every model call as "do
not recommend swinging at these" - so the non-compete was filtering roles on
every evaluation, months after he said to stop. Removed. That entry existed
for no other reason, so leaving the company on the list would have kept the
filter and only hidden the justification.

His second point reframes what the list is for: it should be employers he
would never consider, and he alone should decide what is on it. It had drifted
into a graveyard for roles that were passed on or closed - REI, Kelly
Services, Starz and Unilever are all PASSED or CLOSED in the pipeline anyway,
and their presence here permanently suppresses any future role at those
companies. A role that did not work out is a fact about the role, not the
employer.

So the prompt framing says that outright now: a permanent personal exclusion,
not a record of outcomes, do not infer a reason for an entry, do not extend it
to related companies, and never add to it. The Profile control is relabelled
"Never consider" with help text saying the same, since a list called "ruled
out" invites exactly the drift that happened.

The remaining sixteen are his call. Several are role-level notes rather than
employers - "Mars (Director-level step-down)" suppresses Mars entirely though
a VP role there would be fine - but pruning those is his judgement, not mine.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: The console crawls the app, and Settings holds the wiring
entries.body:
Two corrections from Dan, both of which I had backwards.

He asked whether the console could go beyond a page he gave it. I read that as
a security worry and narrowed it. He meant it as a feature request. So it
crawls now: give it a starting path and it follows the links the app itself
renders, breadth first, up to twelve pages, with the whole context capped at
90k characters and each page's share shrinking as more arrive. One page can
answer "is this panel confusing"; only several can answer "is this app
coherent", which is the question worth asking.

Bounded by what a person could click. Only <a> hrefs are followed - matching
every href attribute swept up the stylesheet, the HMR chunk, the manifest and
two favicons, and the first six-page crawl came back having read one real page
and five assets. Assets, /_next, /api and the sign-out link are all excluded;
following logout would have signed him out mid-prompt.

And he was right that the calendar URL and the Drive folder id do not belong on
Profile. Profile holds what the app knows about him; those are wiring, like the
model. Moved, not copied, with the same formData.has() guard - a field absent
from a form reads as empty, so without it, saving his profile would have
blanked his calendar subscription and sent every future document to a brand new
Drive folder. parseDriveFolderId moved to a shared module rather than being
copied, and the settings form now refuses a paste that does not parse instead
of quietly clearing the folder Counsel has been filing into.

Each of the four fields now has exactly one editor, verified by checking which
page renders which input.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Block API paths in the console, and delete three queries nobody reads
entries.body:
Dan asked whether giving the console a root path would let it go beyond that.
It would not - it fetches one page once, the model has no tools and cannot
make a request of its own, and the path is validated to a single leading slash
so it cannot leave the origin. But "a path" is broader than "a page", and one
GET handler here is not read-only: the Google OAuth callback upserts a
connection. It needs a valid code so a typed path could not really do
anything, which is not a property worth relying on from a text box. /api is
now rejected outright - the console attaches pages, and an endpoint returns
JSON that says nothing about the interface anyway.

The lint sweep then turned up something worth more than "unused variable".
Three of those unused names were results of database queries inside the
Promise.all on Today and Pipeline: every load of either page was fetching
deleted applications, recent job mail and a noise count, and discarding all
three. Residue from the route split, invisible because a wasted query looks
exactly like a fast one.

Also removed, all dead since the pipeline table moved to its own route:
renderRow, renderCard, the archive grouping they fed, and six unused imports
across both pages. page.tsx is 787 lines to 726.

Verified by diffing the rendered pages before and after: both are byte
identical, 80,327 and 172,877 bytes, same visible text, same role-link counts.
Nothing removed was reachable.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: A settings page with a console for asking a model about the app itself
entries.body:
Every model surface here is grounded and narrow on purpose: the assistant sees
one role, Ask sees the search snapshot, the review sees a document. None of
them can see the app, which is why "this panel has twenty-six controls and no
state" was a diagnosis Dan had to drag out of me by getting confused first.

/settings has a prompt box wired to any model, Claude or Gemini, with one
capability beyond a plain prompt: it can attach a real page from the app. The
route fetches it same-origin with the caller's own session, strips the scripts
so the RSC payload cannot pass off unrendered props as content, and hands over
the visible text plus an inventory of every control in document order. Counting
buttons is exactly what a person will not do by hand.

Read only, no tools, and the path is validated to a single leading slash - a
console that will fetch any URL is an SSRF hole whether or not there is one
user. Runs are kept in ConsoleRun for the same reason AskLog exists: a critique
worth having is worth finding again.

Also moved rather than copied: the default model control was on /profile, which
holds the content that grounds the AI, not the machinery. Two editors over one
field is how a stale form silently reverts it. saveProfile now only writes
preferredModel when the form actually carries it - without that guard, saving
the profile would have reset his model choice to the default every time, which
is the same class of bug as a repair that rebuilds content from an empty
string.

On its first real run against the Coca-Cola role it found two things I had
missed: a zeroed "Pay Range: 0 USD - 0 USD" scrape artifact, which turns out to
affect 3 job descriptions with 9 more carrying duplicate pay blocks, and the
split-verdict UI shipped yesterday giving no cue which of two disagreeing
verdicts is authoritative.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Enforce the never-drop list in code, and put the narrative-only facts in the variants
entries.body:
Dan: "I think YOU should say this should be a global fix, I don't want to have
to fix every single resume I generate." Correct, and two of the required
proofs were still being dropped on every role.

The cause of one is the oldest lesson in CLAUDE.md. The PCI descoping, the
privacy work and the email and SMS portfolio existed ONLY in careerNarrative,
and generation tailors from the VARIANT - so no prompt instruction could
reliably surface them, the same way a variant missing LEGO produces a resume
missing LEGO. They are bullets in all four variants now, stated as scope with
no figures and no outcomes, because none are recorded.

Change and transformation management was already in every variant and named on
the never-drop list, and was still cut on three roles out of three. So the
list is now checked instead of asked for: MUST_INCLUDE tests the returned
roles for eight required proofs and retries once naming what went missing,
with the instruction to merge rather than cut if the budget is tight. It does
not block the way a missing employer does - a resume light one proof is still
a resume, and the review catches the rest.

Three roles went from 14/16 each to 15, 15 and 16 of 16, and the item that
slips is now different each time rather than the same two every time.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Stop resumes silently dropping an employer, and stop selection re-dropping the same material
entries.body:
Dan, on why every resume needs the same fixes: "i am a 30+ year senior
executive looking for a job in a market that is brutal, i want these resumes
and cover letters to be the best and never omit the breth of what i did."
Three faults were in the way.

A WHOLE EMPLOYER GOING MISSING. Two identical requests for the Capital One
role: one returned Delta and Charter, the next returned Charter alone. Nine
years at Delta, gone, and the document would have saved and synced to Drive
without complaint because a one-employer resume is structurally valid. It
recurs on roughly one generation in three and hit twice in a row once.
missingEmployers() now checks the output against the employers the base lists,
retries up to three times naming what was dropped, and if it still comes back
incomplete returns an error and saves nothing. A missing resume costs a click;
a resume missing a decade costs an application.

SELECTION RE-DROPPING THE SAME MATERIAL. Across three roles, 10 of 17 review
findings were omissions of material the base already had - email and SMS gone
from two of three, the marketing budget and org measures from two of three,
plus the serviceability story, 24x7 operations, the Executive Readiness
Accelerator and change management. All sixteen bullet slots were equal, so the
model re-decided from scratch each time. standingPreferences now names the
never-drop material, with the rule that carries it: where the budget is tight,
MERGE two facts into one bullet rather than cutting either. Breadth survives
merging and does not survive cutting.

DUPLICATION I INTRODUCED. Vendor ownership was being claimed three times in
one draft and the agency years rendered both as a company block and under
Earlier Experience. Both fixed by a say-each-thing-once rule; verified at 1 and
2 mentions with no duplicate block.

Also raised max_tokens to 12,000, which was still set for a one-page resume.

Honest state: the never-drop list took two roles from missing several items to
13 and 14 of 16. It is a prompt, so it is a request - change management and the
PCI/privacy proof still drop, and the review is what catches those.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Fixing one finding no longer throws away the rest
entries.body:
Dan: "fix is working but you have to run check it after each individual fix,
it's odd." It was. Every refine cleared the whole findings list, so working
through three findings cost three checks at about twenty-five seconds each,
and the list vanished under him between them.

A targeted single-finding fix rarely invalidates the other findings, so they
now stay and only the one just applied drops off. A bulk rewrite still clears
everything, because everything moved.

What it will not do is pretend the remainder is still verified: a line above
the list says a fix has landed since it was made, and an emptied list reads
"every finding has been fixed, none of it is verified yet" rather than the
clean bill of health that wording implied before.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: The title guard was adding a title that was already there
entries.body:
It compared the base's "Vice President, Digital Marketing & eCommerce" against
the model's "VP, Digital Marketing & eCommerce" as a plain substring, decided
the title was missing, and helpfully added it a second time - so the heading
read "Charter Communications | Vice President, Digital Marketing & eCommerce |
VP, Digital Marketing & eCommerce | Cable and broadband operator".

Matching is normalised now: vice president and VP, senior and sr, & and and,
punctuation and spacing folded away. Verified on three cases - abbreviated,
spelled out, and genuinely absent - where only the last one repairs.

Worth noting the shape of this, since it is the second time today. A guard
written to catch a model omission introduced its own defect, because it
assumed the model would phrase things exactly as the source does. A repair
that fires when it should not is not obviously safer than the bug it fixes.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: A promotion reads as a diff: the scope line, and a title that cannot vanish
entries.body:
Dan asked whether there was a more elegant way to show how his scope expanded
from Director to Managing Director. There was, and building it turned up a
defect that had been shipping quietly.

markdown-lite gains "> Domain · Domain · Domain": the remit under a title,
smaller and grey, directly above that title's bullets. Two titles with two
bullet lists show that someone was promoted but not what changed; a sentence
would spend a bullet on org-chart mechanics. A scope line lets the reader do
the comparison - Strategy, Budget and Capability Delivery arrive, Email
Deployment and Project Management go.

The shed is the point, and the narrative now says so. What Dan described is
not scope handed to him: as Director he ran project management and day-to-day
email deployment, began building the agile product delivery capability
alongside the organisation it would replace, and deliberately transitioned the
Salesforce architects into IT to stand up a COE. At the reorg he gave up the
project-management team and the email specialists and took on strategy and the
budget. Gaining strategy while shedding execution is the executive move and
must never be written as a reduction. Recorded with the exact claim protected:
Delta's first MARKETING agile product delivery capability - Delta had agile in
IT, so the qualifier is what makes it defensible.

The defect: a role returned with no subroles renders its bullets straight
under the employer line, so nine years as VP, Digital Marketing & eCommerce
came out as "Charter Communications" and a list of bullets, with the title
nowhere on the page. The schema asks for it now, and asking is not a
guarantee, so withTitle() repairs it deterministically from the base variant's
"### Title | Employer" lines. It refuses when an employer has two titles,
because the bullets could belong to either.

Same rule as the cover-letter loss: when the model omitting something yields a
silently wrong document rather than an error, repair it in code.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: The resume is two pages, and the rule was written in four places
entries.body:
The single-page limit was deleting Dan's best evidence. Generation had to
choose between the Adobe replatform, the serviceability work measured by order
completion, the #2 channel at 3M+ transactions, the org built from zero to 32
and the 500-person SAFe transformation, and it dropped four of the five. The
document ran to about 1.4 pages regardless, so the rule cost content and
bought nothing.

A two-page draft carried all of them plus the vendor ownership and change
management he supplied today, with no invented figures - and surfaced material
that had never survived a cut, including the Akamai lead-capture fallback that
turned a downstream billing outage into a deferred conversion rather than a
dark storefront.

Length is replaced by a bar rather than removed, because two pages with no
constraint is how a resume fills with adjectives and this model manufactures
an outcome whenever it is asked to add something. At most 16 bullets, each
carrying a verified figure or a named system, platform, scope or organisation;
no bare fragments where a bullet belongs; page one holds the strongest
material.

The per-title cap scales with tenure. A flat five trimmed Charter - nine years
and five hero stories - as hard as a six-month Managing Director title. Five
normally, seven for a tenure of five years or more.

The rule turned out to live in four places, and changing the Profile alone
would have left three contradicting it: standingPreferences twice, the
generate-documents tool schema plus a hard PER_ROLE/TOTAL budget in code, and
the review prompt, which scores against it and was calling a two-page resume
blocking. A preference duplicated into code is not a preference.

Also recorded, from Dan: he owned all technology and strategic vendor
relationships at Delta across BOTH roles with scope expanding on promotion,
all technology vendors at Charter for the ATG and Adobe stack, and change and
transformation management at Delta. None of it was written down anywhere,
which is why the review kept raising it. It is in all four variants and the
narrative now, stated as ownership with no figure and no outcome, because none
is recorded.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Stop the fix pass inventing an outcome for every capability it adds
entries.body:
Running the whole loop on the Coca-Cola CRM role answered the question it was
built for, in both directions. The fixes landed: the cover letter no longer
claims Atlanta is home when the property is sold, it names the domain gap
plainly instead of hedging about vendor relationships, it states the June
restructuring and immediate availability, and it names what Coca-Cola actually
operates. That is a letter worth sending against one that was not.

And the same pass invented a claim. Told to add the Workfront and Aha! work it
wrote "to cut cycle time and get campaigns to market faster" - the tools are
his, the outcome was measured by nobody. The resume did it too, attaching
"measured by marketing's contribution to revenue and conversion rate" to a
bullet that had no measure. Roughly one per run, and always the same reflex:
asked to add a capability, justify it with a result.

"Do not invent new claims" had been in that prompt from the start and was
ignored every time. Naming the exact pattern with the real failing sentence,
and saying what to do instead - name the tool and stop - took three runs of the
same instruction from inventing to clean. Also added: a "measured by" clause
may only name a measure present in the source, and an instruction that cannot
be carried out without inventing should be carried out partially rather than
completely and falsely.

The letter is saved with the invented clause struck and the base resume's own
phrasing in its place, synced to Drive, with the previous version intact
behind it.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Keep Check reachable, and stop a save from closing the document
entries.body:
Two faults, both mine from today, both showing up as "Check it doesn't show
again" after applying a fix and saving.

The status line said "Rewritten, not checked since" while the only button was
Save changes. I had made Save, Fix and Check mutually exclusive, so the moment
there were unsaved edits the check disappeared - exactly when the line was
telling him to use it. A status that names an action has to leave that action
on screen, so Check now stays as a secondary control whenever the document has
not been checked.

And the document itself was closing. `open={openDoc === type}` went on the
<details> this morning so the URL could expand one; React re-syncs that
attribute on re-render, so the router.refresh() after saving snapped shut a
document opened by hand, taking the whole editor with it. It is
`open={... || undefined}` now: forced open when the URL asks, and otherwise
uncontrolled exactly as it was before the URL could open one.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Rework the document panel into a state and one action
entries.body:
Dan: "I don't know how I am supposed to work with this at all." He was right,
and the inventory was the diagnosis - roughly twenty-six controls on one
expanded document, most of them added today, each a patch for the confusion
the previous one caused. Four words for one operation: review, check, refine,
fix. Two of those I had introduced to disambiguate the others.

It is now one status line and one action. The status answers what to do next
(not checked / 3 to fix, 1 needs you / rewritten, not checked since / checked,
nothing found) and the primary button is whatever that next step is: Save
changes when there are unsaved edits, otherwise Fix N, otherwise Check it.
Everything occasional - the text itself, downloads, Drive, a manual
instruction, versions, delete - moved behind More. Five visible controls
instead of twenty-six, measured on the Coca-Cola cover letter.

Deleted rather than added: the compare panel's review and its duplicate Fix
buttons are gone, so checking exists in exactly one place, and the two "Review
the ..." links I put in the top row this morning are gone with them. They were
a patch for the review being hard to find, and the document stating its own
status solves that without two more buttons.

And the part Dan asked for, which is a safety property rather than a nicety.
He has no figures beyond his verified metrics, so a finding like "add a
measure to this bullet" cannot be carried out from the record - handing it to
a rewriter is asking a model to invent a number, which is the single worst
thing this feature could do. Findings now carry needsHim and a specific
question. Those are excluded from "Fix N" by the code rather than by asking
the model nicely; answering inserts the answer verbatim, and "I don't have
that" stops the impossible question being raised again.

Also: an empty review is now confirmed with a second pass before it is shown.
"Nothing found" reads as a confident verdict and is the answer most likely to
stop him looking - and a cover letter that three consecutive runs each found
six problems in, including a claim that Atlanta is home when it is not, came
back clean once.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Version the icon URLs, so a corrected icon actually reaches the phone
entries.body:
The 180px touch icon shipped broken, was fixed, deployed, and the phone went
on showing the old one after the home-screen icon was deleted and re-added.
iOS caches the touch icon per URL and keeps it well past the web clip that
pulled it, so a new file at the same path is never fetched.

Every icon URL now carries ?v=2, which also clears any copy held by the CDN.
The manifest icons carry it too, since iOS 17 reads those as well.

Bump the number whenever the artwork changes. Nothing else forces a refetch.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Freeze changelog

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Only the fix you clicked says it is running
entries.body:
Clicking one "Fix this" turned every button in the list into "Fixing..." at
once, which reads as having started all of them. Only the clicked one ever
ran: the handler passes that finding's text and nothing else issues a request.
But the label came from a single shared flag, so there was no way to tell
which fix was being applied, or that the others were merely blocked.

Both panels now track WHICH control is running rather than that one is. The
others still disable, because two refines racing on the same document would
overwrite each other, but a disabled button no longer claims to be working.

entries.author: Dan Curis

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Put the review where it can be found, and make its findings act everywhere
entries.body:
Dan ran the comparison, saw blocking findings, and asked how to apply them.
The answer was that he was in the wrong panel - which is a design fault, not a
user error. Two surfaces said "review", the one in the top action row could
only report, and the one that could actually fix anything was hidden behind a
disclosure triangle on a document. He used the one he could see.

That is the Ask-button lesson again, from this same file: he is the only user,
so a control he cannot see does not exist. Three changes:

- "Review the resume" and "Review the cover letter" now sit in the top row
  beside Compare. They are links carrying ?doc=<type>&review=1, so they expand
  that document and start its review there. The URL rather than client state
  because the top row has to reach into a component it does not own, and
  because the back button and a link to himself on a phone both then work.
  The effect that runs it is guarded by a ref: a review is a paid call and an
  effect that re-fires would spend money quietly.
- The comparison stops calling itself a review. Its button is "What is wrong
  with each resume", so "review" means one thing in this app, and the label
  says resumes because that is all it compares.
- Its findings now carry working "Fix this" buttons, on either draft. The
  refine route takes content explicitly rather than reading the stored row,
  which is what lets the unsaved alternative be rewritten at all; the document
  id only supplies the role and posting for grounding. The current draft
  becomes editable here too and grows a "Save these fixes" button once one has
  been applied, and Close reads "Discard and close" while a fix is unsaved.

Lint caught the thing worth catching: currentCoverLetter was unused, and
keeping the alternative writes its cover letter as well - a document the
comparison never shows. It now says so under the button, with both word
counts, rather than replacing it silently.

Verified server-side: the links render, ?doc=cover_letter opens that document
and no other. The click-through is not verified - the session cookie is
httpOnly and the token also authenticates production, so it does not belong in
a browser-automation transcript.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Make the review's fixes actually apply, and admit the rewrite is a proposal
entries.body:
Dan ran a review on the Coca-Cola CRM letter, saw the blocking findings, and
asked whether it adds in what is missing. It did not, and worse, the way to
make it do so was not where he was looking.

Two surfaces render findings and only one could act on them. The compare panel
listed the problems and threw away the `fix` the model had already written for
each - not a design choice, an omission. It shows them now, and says where
they get applied, since it deliberately has no refine of its own: that view is
for choosing between two drafts.

In the editor, "Use this fix" only filled the refine box. It read like it
applied the fix; the document was untouched until you noticed the box, ran
refine, and then saved. Three steps, the first of which looked like all three.
It is "Fix this" now and applies immediately, with "Edit first" kept for when
the instruction needs adjusting, and "Fix all N blocking" for the whole set.
Blocking first, because offering to fix everything on a list whose tail is
stylistic invites a rewrite nobody asked for.

`refine` had to take the instruction as an argument. setInstruction is
asynchronous, so a handler that set it and then called refine would have sent
whatever was in the box before, which is usually nothing.

The honest part: a refine does not reliably apply what it was asked to. The
same letter with the same three blocking findings, twice: one pass removed the
"Atlanta is home for me" line the finding was about, the other left it in
place. Clearing the findings after a rewrite was already right, since they
describe replaced text, but blank implied the work was done. It now says the
document has been rewritten and not re-checked, and that a refine does not
always apply every fix.

Verified the chain end to end against the live Coca-Cola letter: review
returned 3 blocking findings, the assembled instruction went to refine, the
letter changed, and nothing was written to the database, which is what makes
the rewrite safe to read before saving.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Document the review pass and the cover letter loss
entries.body:
Both are the kind of thing CLAUDE.md exists for: a design decision whose
obvious alternative is wrong, and a data loss where every individual step
succeeded.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Restore the 56 cover letters the sign-off repair emptied, and stop it recurring
entries.body:
The bulk review pass found three empty cover letters, which turned out to be
56. Every one of them was two lines: "Sincerely," and "Daniel Curis".

How it happened. Most of those letters were never written here - they were
adopted from Drive, and an adopted Document deliberately stores content: ""
because the file is the record. The sign-off repair rebuilt every cover letter
as letterhead + body + sign-off without checking there was a body, so an empty
one became 26 characters. That row now had content, so the ordinary Drive sync
did exactly what it is designed to do and rendered those 26 characters over
the real .docx and .pdf. Nothing failed. The rows saved, the uploads
succeeded, and every letter was correctly signed.

It was survivable only because Drive keeps its own revisions, which the
one-file-per-document-type design had been quietly resting on. All 56 .docx
files had a pre-incident revision.

scripts/restore-cover-letters.ts puts each one back: the original .docx byte
for byte, its text extracted into the Document row, and the .pdf either
restored the same way (20 of them) or re-rendered from the recovered text (36,
which had no PDF in Drive before the repair created one). All 56 recovered,
shortest 1,952 characters, median 2,692. Nothing had gone out in the meantime:
the only correspondence since is one AT&T draft with no attachments.

Storing the text is the durable half of the fix. These letters existed only as
files, which is why a repair that rebuilt content from an empty string could
destroy them with nothing to compare against.

Two guards, since the empty-content check in syncDocumentToDrive did not catch
this - by the time the sync ran the content was not empty, it was wrong:

- syncDocumentToDrive refuses to upload a resume or cover letter under 600
  characters. The shortest real letter here is about 1,950, so the floor is
  far below anything genuine and still catches a sign-off standing alone.
- audit.ts gains "Document too short to be real", because this surfaced only
  because a review happened to read one months later.

And the audit check that motivated the original repair was itself wrong. It
tested for a sign-off word anywhere in the body, so a bare "Best," - how
twenty of the pre-Counsel letters actually close - read as unsigned. It is now
anchored to its own line near the end. A false positive there is not cosmetic:
it is what prompted a bulk rewrite of 69 documents.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Make the split verdicts reachable from the pipeline
entries.body:
Seven roles already had one and the only way to find them was opening ninety
roles one at a time, which is the same fault as a count that links nowhere -
the disagreements are the entire reason for paying for a second provider.

A banner states the number and filters the list to exactly those rows, so the
count and its destination come from one definition and cannot drift. The
pipeline query now takes four evaluations rather than one and carries the
model, because a disagreement between providers is invisible in a single row.

`split` is a URL flag rather than another Stage. A stage is exclusive and a
split is orthogonal: a shortlisted role can be split, and folding it into the
enum would make it stop being shortlisted.

The filtered view says what it is filtered to and offers a way back. Without
that, seven rows just looked like the pipeline.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: Cross-check a stretch verdict, and say which way the two models split
entries.body:
The second opinion only fired on pass, on the reasoning that closing a role
must not rest on one opinion. That left the genuinely uncertain verdict
unchecked, which is backwards: a confident swing needs no help, but a stretch
is the model saying "maybe", and it is exactly where the other provider's read
changes what Dan does with his week. It now runs on stretch too. Only pass
still moves the status, because how promising two models find a role is not
where the application actually is.

The disagreement also needed a direction. The panel showed both verdicts with
a "disagrees" chip, which reads identically whether the second opinion was
warmer or colder - and those call for opposite actions. describeSplit names
the action instead: swing over stretch is "worth moving up the week", pass
under stretch is "worth a look before you spend the effort", swing against
pass is the widest they get and gets neither.

It is derived from the evaluation rows on the page rather than returned by the
evaluate call, so it survives the refresh that call triggers and is still
there tomorrow. Two runs of the SAME model differing returns null: that is
sampling noise, not a second opinion, and presenting it as one would overstate
what the app knows.

Seven roles in the pipeline already have a live split, including two Coca-Cola
roles and GoTo Foods where Gemini says swing and Sonnet says stretch.

entries.author: Dan Curis
entries.subject: A second model reviews the draft, and reports findings rather than a winner
entries.body:
The obvious version of this was a bake-off: generate with both providers and
ask which is stronger. That is a taste judgement with no ground truth, it is
dominated by self-preference (each model picks its own draft), and it would
not have caught a single defect these documents have actually shipped. Every
one of those was specific and checkable: a metric that is not on the verified
list, a hero story the variant had and the draft dropped, ten bullets on a
single-page resume, a letter that never names what the employer operates.

So the reviewer gets the posting, the base resume the draft was tailored from
and the house rules, and returns findings. Each carries a fix written as an
instruction, so it drops into the refine box that already exists: "the posting
names CDP ownership three times and the resume never says CDP" is something to
act on, where "version B is better" leaves nothing to do.

It runs on the other provider. Document.model records who wrote each version
so reviewerFor() can pick the opposite one, because a model grading its own
output agrees with its own choices.

Two things it caught on its first real run, both fixed in the Profile row
rather than in prompts, and both live already since profile edits need no
deploy:

- standingPreferences listed "Modernised" among the approved verbs, so the
  house style was instructing British spelling into a US executive search.
  Five more were in positioning, careerNarrative and evaluationFramework.
- The verified-metrics list permits the figure 500 without saying what it may
  attach to, so "500-person SAFe transformation" was being written as "ran a
  500-person delivery organization" - in the resume and the cover letter both.
  Positioning now says a figure keeps its noun. Regenerating produced the
  correct claim in both documents.

The first draft of the prompt reported the markup as a fault: it read "##
Daniel Curis" as a casing error and " :: " as a broken separator, when the
renderer applies uppercase, navy and right-alignment at render time. An audit
that cries wolf gets ignored, so the prompt now states the storage contract
and rules presentation out of scope.
